Can an Agent Own an Entire Simulation-Based Design Workflow?

Once humans and AI have agreed on the requirements, can an agent take continuing responsibility for the design iterations that follow? I tried this with two simulation toys—an airfoil and a battery module—across 30 runs and 900 evaluation steps. The loop could improve designs through feedback. Yet all 12 battery-agent runs found feasible designs, while the original system selected a feasible final candidate in only six; a high-scoring airfoil trajectory also failed its ride-height perturbation check. Batch 1 closed the “change parameters—read feedback” loop. It did not close the loop of taking responsibility for the evidence an engineering objective needs next. That is the responsibility I want to hand over.

Part 1 | What Happens If I Give an Agent the Engineering Objective Directly?

The idea: a design process that evidence can keep correcting

My full hypothesis is this: could an agent system start from a rocket's mission requirements, a racing driver's characteristics, or a battery's intended use, and organise modelling, simulation, search and validation? There is a definite order. First, work with people to translate needs into engineering objectives. Then establish what evidence and evaluation metrics would demonstrate success. Next, choose parameters, models and experiments under exploration and budget constraints. Finally, interpret simulation results, revise hypotheses, and carry that updated understanding into the next iteration.

NASA's system-design process connects stakeholder expectations, requirements definition, logical decomposition and design-solution iteration, allowing inconsistent results to send the team upstream. I use that recursive structure as the basis for the human–agent responsibilities explored here. Source: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, Figure 4.0-1.

Source: NASA Figure 4.0-1 ↗Open full-size adaptation ↗

Human–AI roles and the simulation / physical evidence branches are my additions. This is a hypothesis about full responsibility, not NASA’s AI proposal or an implemented Batch 1 capability. Scroll within the figure on narrow screens.

The adaptation preserves the original positions and direction: expectations at the upper left, requirements at the upper right, decomposition at the lower right, solution iteration below the centre, and recursion or product realisation on the left. My hypothesis overlays this structure: humans and AI jointly own the first two stages; after requirements are anchored, the agent owns simulation iterations within its authority, while people review direction and results. Physical manufacturing, test operations and real-world risks still require human involvement. If new evidence makes the requirements infeasible or calls for changing the objective, the agent returns the issue to that joint definition process.

There is a parallel with coding agents: tools turn actions into observable feedback, and the task drives the next move. Physical design adds a further question. Passing tests can show that software meets those tests; passing a simulation still leaves us asking how much reality the model represents. The optimiser sees a selected slice of the world, not the world itself.

What interests me is the possibility of an agent continuously maintaining one overall objective across judgements normally distributed among roles. Human teams can also optimise jointly. The hypothesis is not that people cannot do this, but that a low-intervention system might coordinate requirements, physics, experiments and cost more continuously, without losing constraints at handoffs.

For the first batch, I fixed the requirements, design space and simulation tools, then asked whether the loop could make progress. Next, I want to transfer experimental strategy, fidelity selection, information gathering and belief updates one at a time, before returning to the quality of human–AI requirement definition. Jointly anchoring requirements is the entry point, not a human step that must eventually disappear. This also makes failure easier to locate: a weak proposal, a tool blind to an important variable, or evidence that never changes the decision?

The comparisons in this batch

Each scenario has five groups—A, B, C, B-nomem and C-nomem—with three starting points and 30 steps per run. A uses Nelder–Mead. B uses an LLM with metrics, numerical checks and errors. C additionally receives selected physical-field features. The nomem variants remove pre-sweep experience, not within-run history.

I wanted to observe whether an LLM could keep using feedback, whether field features changed its judgements, and whether prior experience changed exploration. A has no pre-sweep information; in the battery task it stays at low fidelity, whereas B/C can call high fidelity. This is therefore an exploration of mechanisms, not an algorithm ranking under matched information and cost. A fairer comparison must account for model calls, solver cost, caches, retries and an independent validation budget.

Part 2 | Two-Dimensional Aerodynamics: More Downforce, but a Gap in Acceptance

A. The problem and real-world considerations

This is not a complete racing front wing. It is an inverted airfoil section operating near the ground. The task is to increase downforce while penalising drag above an agreed threshold. The agent can change ride height h/c, installation angle α and maximum camber m. Thickness, camber position, Reynolds number, turbulence model and the two-dimensional steady-state assumption are fixed by a human.

Interaction between the ground and wing means the same section behaves differently at different heights. A real vehicle's height does not remain constant either. Nominal performance is therefore only the first question; obtaining usable results after a small displacement is the second. Batch 1 placed that second question in an independent post-search check: h/c is shifted by ±0.01, without returning those results to the agent.

B. The AutoResearch trajectory: what exactly is the curve optimising?

The earlier label “trusted objective score” collapsed two operations. The clearer definition is: first pass numerical checks, then calculate the aerodynamic objective J. “Trusted” is not an LLM's confidence score for a design.

Simulation calculates surface forces and normalises them by dynamic pressure and reference area to obtain lift and drag coefficients, Cₗ and Cᴅ. For the inverted section, Cₗ is negative, so −Cₗ represents downforce. This project defines:

Aerodynamic objective — higher is betterJ = −Cₗ − 10 × max(0, Cᴅ − 0.06)Cₗ = Fᵧ / (½ρU∞²S), Cᴅ = Fₓ / (½ρU∞²S). The threshold 0.06 and weight 10 are preset design trade-offs, not fluid-mechanics constants.

Below the drag threshold, J equals the downforce coefficient. Above it, an extra 0.01 in drag coefficient costs 0.1 points. This is a scalar objective with a drag penalty, not a hard constraint that rejects every over-budget design. Convergence, residuals, force stability, near-wall y⁺ and mesh checks must also pass before a result enters the curve.

The green staircase records the largest J so far. Dots are accepted numerical results; crosses below the plot mark evaluations without a score. The horizontal axis includes cache hits. The horizontal references come from two other project records—not the initial design or a known global optimum.

The grey dashed line, 1.093, is the best known result in the pre-search parameter sweep: h/c=0.35, α=5°, m=0.04. A summary of that sweep was available to B/C groups with memory. It shows where the project had already looked; it is not a hidden test answer. The purple dash-dot line, 0.891, is A-s0's best result after 30 Nelder–Mead evaluations from the same starting point. The initial design scores 0.767; the numerical baseline scores 0.891 after optimisation. It is higher because it has already been optimised. “Baseline” does not mean “starting design” here.

C-s0 set nine records over 30 steps, increasing J from 0.767 to 1.248. Both its initial and best designs stay below the drag threshold, so this increase directly reflects greater nominal downforce. By changing height, angle and camber, the agent found a better candidate under the current model. That is the first useful result demonstrated by this AutoResearch trajectory.

C. Physical fields and independent probes: what changed behind the score?

Left: step 0. Right: step 23. These plots post-process archived OpenFOAM meshes, pressure p and velocity U; no simulation was rerun. Axes and colour scales are shared. Colours use original cell values; streamlines are interpolated from the steady velocity field.

View the full-size airfoil fields

The top row shows Cₚ: pressure distribution and suction near the wing. The bottom row shows speed and streamlines: the ground gap, flow around the section and wake. Surface pressure and viscous forces integrate into forces, then Cₗ and Cᴅ, and finally J. The field plot helps explain why the objective changes; the search curve records how much it changes. They tell one connected story.

Here h/c rises from 0.3000 to 0.5621, α from 2° to 4.5°, and m from 0.040 to 0.075. Downforce increases from 0.767 to 1.248, while drag also rises from 0.0173 to 0.0323. Several variables changed together. Attributing a contribution to one variable requires controlled perturbations, not just visual comparison.

The next table brings nominal performance, small operating changes and numerical checks together. It corresponds to Part 1's independent evaluation, not an extra search reward.

What do the numerical checks actually test?
  • Convergence and residuals: solver stop status; post-processing accepts final residuals up to ten times the control thresholds. Airfoil acceptance limits are 10⁻³ for p and 10⁻⁴ for velocity and turbulence quantities.
  • Force stability: mean Cₗ in two consecutive 100-iteration windows must differ by no more than 1% × max(|final Cₗ|, 0.1). This is not a statistical confidence interval.
  • Wall and mesh: mean airfoil y⁺ within 1–300; maximum non-orthogonality ≤70°, maximum skewness ≤4, and no Failed mesh checks.
  • Both height perturbations returned not_settled / residual_stall after 6,000 iterations. Diagnostic values retain readings from failed solves; they are not accepted objective values.
  • Systematic mesh independence, unsteady-model comparison, and physical calibration remain future evidence requirements.

Both perturbations failed to converge after 6,000 iterations, with failure type not_settled. The table retains the mean force coefficients from the last 100 iterations and a diagnostic J calculated from those means. The original accepted metric remains null. Readings exist, but they have not qualified as stable solutions for ranking. The current simulation workflow did not produce adequate evidence for the best candidate's neighbourhood. The next task is to distinguish steady-solver difficulty, mesh/model sensitivity and actual flow changes—not label a failed computation as physical stall.

Across all 15 airfoil runs, three passed this numerical-computability probe, 11 failed it and one had no valid best candidate. The original field is named robust, but it only requires scoreable results at both perturbations; it sets no bound on performance degradation. Calling this complete engineering robustness would overstate the check.

D. The capability this toy points to: managing missing evidence

Multi-step parameter search can already run in a low-dimensional, fixed-model setting. The next capability is not simply opening more knobs. It is recognising whether the task needs a better design or a better validation experiment next. When neighbouring cases fail, the system needs discriminating numerical experiments, not just more attempts near the same score.

Two dimensions, steady flow, three parameters and a fixed operating point are deliberate limits. Real design adds three-dimensional spanwise effects, whole-vehicle aerodynamic balance, changing conditions, structure and manufacturing. These require mechanisms to change models, extend objectives, run sensitivity studies and independently accept candidates—not merely a larger parameter table.

More field information does not automatically produce a better strategy: C did not consistently outperform B. Runs with pre-sweep memory revisited some known boundaries less often but could move into new failure regions. I therefore want to measure whether each computation changes the next decision, which explanation it eliminates and what it costs—not simply whether failures disappear.

Part 3 | Batteries: The Loop Learns a Trade-Off, but the System May Select the Wrong Endpoint

A. The problem: constrained fast-charging and cooling design

The task is to charge a three-cell air-cooled module from 5% to 50% SOC as quickly as possible while keeping maximum temperature at or below 45°C. Charging stops early if voltage reaches 4.2 V. The agent jointly adjusts constant-current charge rate, channel width and inlet air speed. Faster is not sufficient: stopping before the target SOC or overheating the cells defeats the requirement.

PyBaMM's DFN electrochemical model calculates charging and heat generation. Tier 0 uses a simplified lumped thermal model. Tier 2 uses OpenFOAM's two-dimensional conjugate heat transfer for three cells and two channels, iteratively coupling temperature back to electrochemistry. These levels differ in both cost and model structure. “High fidelity” here is a relative term within this project.

B. The AutoResearch trajectory: enter feasibility, then reduce time

The search maximises a penalised objective Jᵦ. The plot instead selects tier-2 results that pass numerical checks, reach 50% SOC and meet the temperature limit, then expresses their objective as charging minutes.

Search objective — higher is betterJᵦ = −tₘᵢₙ − 50 × max(0, Tₘₐₓ[°C] − 45) − 200 × max(0, 0.5 − SOC)When temperature and charge requirements are met, Jᵦ is negative charging time in minutes. The green line compares times within that feasible set; a short but overheating charge is not counted as progress.

Only numerically accepted tier-2 results with Tₘₐₓ ≤45°C and SOC ≥0.5 are included. Bottom markers retain low-fidelity and constraint-violating evaluations. The 14.3% reduction is relative to this run's first feasible point.

B-s0 first encounters overheating at high fidelity. It then lowers the charge rate and strengthens cooling to become feasible, before gradually increasing the charge rate again. Step 4 yields an 18.000-minute feasible design; step 27 reaches 15.429 minutes, with five improvements to the feasible best. This is a concrete feedback-driven joint optimisation process.

C. Temperature fields and independent probes: how much margin remains?

Left: step 1's tier-2 recheck of the initial design with unchanged design parameters. Right: the best feasible candidate at step 27. Both reach 50% SOC and share a colour scale. Fields come from the archived third coupling pass; coupling passes are numerical iterations, not the charging time axis.

View the full-size battery temperature fields

The question is not just whether the plot has red regions. It is how heat leaves three cells through two channels, where hotspots occur and how far Tmax lies from the threshold. The temperature field supplies Tmax, which determines constraint satisfaction and activates the search penalty. Spatial temperature spread ΔT is also recorded, but has no separate acceptance threshold in this batch.

The initial design uses 2.00 C and 0.10 m/s. It reaches the charge target in 13.50 minutes but heats to 53.30°C. The final design uses 1.75 C and 0.50 m/s, reaching 44.78°C in 15.43 minutes. It is slower but feasible relative to the initial design, and 14.3% faster relative to the first feasible design. Together, those comparisons explain the process: find feasibility, then improve within it.

Old robust=true only means both perturbations are scoreable. At +0.1 C, temperature reaches 46.08°C: engineering feasibility fails.

Numerical gates, diagnostics, and model margin: what is the difference?
  • Five tier-2 gates: convergence, final residuals, coupling convergence, energy balance, and mesh quality. Coupling temperature tolerance is 1.5 K; relative energy-balance tolerance is 10%.
  • These tolerances accept a solve; they do not bound prediction error. A simulated 44.78°C below a 45°C limit does not establish a reliable 0.22°C physical safety margin.
  • Initial and best spatial temperature spreads ΔT are about 12.42 K and 11.51 K. ΔT is recorded without an acceptance threshold here; pressure drop is also not an optimisation reward.
  • Tier 0 has no spatial mesh or equivalent coupling. Some trust fields are directly assigned on the simplified path; they are not equivalent tier-2 checks.
  • Independent perturbations retain the selected tier. Uniform post-hoc tier-2 rechecks are a separate test; the two should not collapse into one robust label.

The best point has only about 0.22°C of nominal temperature margin. In the original charge-rate perturbations, 1.65 C remains feasible, but 1.85 C reaches 46.08°C. Both simulations pass numerical checks, so the old report still says robust=true. There is no mysterious agent failure here. The acceptance field answered “can we compute it?”, while we wanted to know “can we use it?”. Those questions need separate implementations.

A clearer handoff failure appears in the final selections across all 12 battery-agent runs.

The upper row inspects the complete search history; the lower row checks the endpoint actually recommended by the old system. They may refer to different candidates. Uniform high-fidelity rechecking happened after the runs and did not trigger automatic reselection.

The old selector pooled low- and high-fidelity scores. An optimistic low-fidelity score could outrank a candidate already supported by high-fidelity evidence. All 12 runs found feasible designs, but only six delivered candidates that remained feasible under the high-fidelity recheck.

The ability to find feasible designs had outgrown the system's ability to deliver them. The first repair belongs at the connection between candidate identity, model level and acceptance—not in a vague demand that the LLM understand batteries better.

D. Model fidelity must participate in decisions, not just calculations

One structural detail matters: across this task's entire parameter range, tier 0's heat-transfer correlation uses a constant-Nusselt-number branch. Its heat-transfer coefficient changes with channel width, but not air speed. Air speed changes the recorded pressure drop, which is not part of the objective. The cheap model's thermal score therefore scarcely sees this cooling knob; tier 2 supplies spatial flow and heat-transfer feedback.

The capability required is more specific than “use multiple fidelities”. The agent needs to know which design differences a tool can distinguish, and which require a stronger model. Fidelity selection should consider which model actually contains information about the current question, not just whether it is cheaper. This is an observation about the model implementation, not proof that it caused a particular agent action.

This batch does not fully cover lifetime, lithium plating, fan energy, manufacturing cost or calibration to real batteries. Those omissions call for requirement extension, model applicability, evidence uncertainty and safety margins. Wrapping a more complex problem in the same score curve will not create these capabilities automatically.

Blue D1–D6 labels inside modules reference external capabilities without confusing dependencies with data flow. Source sizes, file lists and dependency details are in the appendix.

The controller selects where to continue; the LLM proposes a concrete change; fixed code executes and scores it. AIDE supplies the agent base, interpreter, journal and backend connection. SciPy provides group A's optimiser. Gmsh, OpenFOAM and PyBaMM supply geometry, meshing and physics. My main work is connecting them into a design loop with contracts, records and failure feedback.

Which models and settings drive AutoResearch?

04 / MODEL & RUN CONFIGURATION

Airfoil physicsOpenFOAM simpleFoam; 2-D steady RANS, k–ω SST, Re=4.5×10⁵, moving ground.Humans preset physics and boundary conditions. The Agent adjusts h/c, α, m, and limited recovery settings; it does not autonomously construct a new physical model.
Battery physicsPyBaMM DFN / Chen2020; tier 0 lumped thermal; tier 2 couples to OpenFOAM 2-D conjugate heat transfer.Tier 2 uses quasi-steady temperature–heat fixed-point coupling: three-pass limit, 1.5 K temperature tolerance. It is not full 3-D transient physical validation.

Checked against historical configuration, 30 summaries, and the local CLI adapter; records are in theappendix. Model names are reproduced as logged.

The agent model and the physical model are different layers: the former proposes designs and interprets outcomes; the latter computes their behaviour. B and C do not use different LLMs. They differ in what feedback the same model sees. Run logs identify claude-cli:claude-sonnet-5, invoked through the local Claude CLI. This is the recorded configuration name, not an independent audit of the provider's model version.

There is also a reproducibility detail: the framework sets temperature=0.0, but the local CLI adapter passes only the prompt, output format and model name—not temperature. The accurate record is “framework configured to zero; backend did not forward it”, not a claim of deterministic zero-temperature execution.

This boundary explains the current autonomy. Humans define the variables, models, objective, recovery menu and budget. The agent consumes parent results, history and optional prior experience, then proposes PARAMS, OPTIONS, a hypothesis, prediction and falsification criterion. Fixed rules govern branching, backtracking and fidelity promotion. Writing a falsification criterion has not yet become automatically executing it and tracking hypotheses.

Numerical results enter Journal through EVAL_JSON and are also recorded in an experimental Git lineage. Step 0, group A and automatic promotions do not require an LLM proposal. Every ten recorded cases, a rerun spot-checks reproducibility. At the end, the old selector recommends a candidate, followed by perturbation checks hidden from the agent; battery endpoints are also rechecked uniformly at tier 2 afterwards.

The missing link is not another agent. It is giving validation the power to change candidate eligibility. Recording a failure and withdrawing a recommendation are not automatically connected, and numerical validity is not fully separated from engineering feasibility. Data reaches the report without necessarily reaching the decision.

Part 5 | Scaling Up Means Scaling Bounded Engineering Responsibility

Figure 5 | A proposed architecture: separate search, evidence and release authority

05 / PROPOSED — NOT A BATCH 1 CLAIM
Let strategy explore; keep evidence traceable; let acceptance say no

Proposed responsibility and data boundaries; not implemented, deployed, or tested at scale.

Rectangle: execution moduleEllipse: data artifact→ Producer → artifact → consumer
Solvers can change; candidate identity, evidence contracts, and acceptance boundaries must survive.Open full proposed architecture ↗
Lesson from the airfoilNominal best does not replace condition coverage. Numerical failure calls for more evidence, not an immediate claim of physical failure.
Lesson from the batteryPreserve model identity with observations. Eligibility must consider high-fidelity feasibility and perturbation conditions.
Lesson from executionAccount for failures and retries. Experts enter at task definition, model conflicts, and release risk.

These are design principles and a proposed architecture derived from the toys—not implemented Batch 1 capabilities or established Batch 2 results. With many candidates, solvers and concurrent tasks, the system should still explain why it spends a unit of budget, which candidate owns a piece of evidence, and who can decide a design is ready to deliver.

Principle 1: the objective is a versioned contract, not one sentence in a prompt

Requirements, operating conditions, constraints, variable permissions and acceptance rules should form one traceable contract. The agent may propose amendments, but changing the task, increasing risk or entering a new model domain needs an explicit approval boundary. Experts decide whether the problem has been posed correctly, rather than choosing every parameter for the agent.

Principle 2: cheap models screen; consequential decisions carry enough evidence

The strategy should state what a computation is for: improving a candidate, distinguishing mechanisms, checking boundaries or reducing uncertainty. A design and its evaluations need separate identities. The same design has different evidence under different meshes, models, versions and conditions. Scores cannot be pooled across fidelities without those labels. Model experts define applicability and calibration; the agent allocates budget within its authority.

Principle 3: failures count, and restarts must not erase engineering history

Runs, candidates, calls and attempts need durable identities and terminal states. Register an expensive call before execution; afterwards record wall time, CPU core-hours, peak memory, LLM usage, cache behaviour and failure type. Concurrency needs idempotency keys, leases and retry limits so restarts do not duplicate charges or misattribute physical jobs.

This is not merely operations. Without a cost and failure ledger, we cannot tell whether a strategy explores effectively or compare it under equal budgets. Numerical failures, infrastructure failures and code defects need different handling. Automatic retry is not a universal diagnosis.

Principle 4: acceptance is not the searcher's highest self-awarded score

Public diagnostics can guide search. Independent held-out evaluations belong in a separate acceptance module that checks numerical validity, engineering constraints, perturbation behaviour and evidence completeness. Its output is recommendation eligibility with reasons, not just another high-fidelity score. Failed candidates stay outside the deliverable set. Further search may use public diagnostics, but repeatedly inspected held-out cases must not keep being called independent tests.

Experts also intervene when models extrapolate, evidence conflicts or remaining risk exceeds delegated authority. For consequential designs, physical testing and authorised engineering approval remain distinct stages. An optimiser cannot sign its own safety conclusion.

Principle 5: fix responsibility boundaries, then scale to measured load

The control plane can begin as a modular monolith, with expensive solves on isolated workers. Add remote executors and clusters when real shared use, queues and resource contention justify them. Contracts, call records, evidence storage and acceptance interfaces remain stable while execution locations change.

Before scaling, establish concurrency limits, per-task cost and memory ceilings, validation budgets, recovery targets, retention and access rules—not just a service diagram. Private evaluation data and design IP need real isolation; solver versions, dependencies and licences must be auditable. Without measured scale, I do not claim an existing node count, throughput or availability level.

Batch 1 does not answer whether an agent can independently design a rocket, racing car or battery. It has changed what I want to test next. Parameter search is one part. A genuinely end-to-end system must also help define the problem, choose informative experiments, manage model differences and recognise when evidence is sufficient—or when it must ask for help.

Agent ownership does not mean removing people from the flowchart. It means knowing which judgements the system can make, which conclusions lack evidence and which risks must return to humans.

Published numeric readings, model records and source hashes: display evidence. Private source paths and raw simulation files are not published. The separate post-run recheck script has no verified LOC count. Design-fragment checks are lightweight string rules, not an industrial security sandbox.

Results come from the existing Batch 1 records of 12 September 2026. This article reorganises their explanation, reads the original perturbation outputs and generates displays; it adds no optimisation or simulation runs. Search curves are representative trajectories. A best-so-far line cannot fall by definition; it is not model training and does not replace all-run comparisons, expert baselines or matched-cost evaluation. Raw-field plots retain their original data. This English edition follows the approved Chinese revision.
